before.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
before.note: Icicle Creek Rd approach into the Enchantments (Alpine Lakes Wilderness); overnight permit required.
before.directions: From US-2 at the western edge of Leavenworth, turn onto Icicle Creek Road and drive 8.4 miles, then turn left onto Eightmile Road (FS Road 7601) and follow the rough dirt road 3.7 miles to the Stuart Lake Trailhead at about 3,400 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park and overnight trips May 15 to Oct 31 need an Enchantment permit; the road is usually gated November into May.

before.name: Gnome Tarn
before.directions: Take the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail, cross Mountaineer Creek and climb to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass, about 2,000 ft of loose scree in 1.25 miles, then cross the Core past Tranquil and Isolation lakes and go cross-country north over slabs and talus to Gnome Tarn below Prusik's south face.

before.name: Prusik Peak
before.directions: Walk up from the tarn to the west end of the south face, find the outside corner where it turns onto the west side, and walk about 100 ft right along the base to the start. Four pitches, about 450 ft, of crack, slab, face and corner climbing reach the West Ridge; the route tops out on the ridge rather than at the summit.

before: From the summit, descend the north face on four single-rope rappels using a single 60m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground to the climbers’ path; two optional rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully can replace that downclimb. The first rap station is an old bolt at the true summit (reported to predate the 1980s); the second rappel is built around a wedged block that looks sketchy but has held for decades of parties. Remaining stations are slung natural anchors (webbing/tat) — carry extra material to back up aged slings. From the climbers’ path, scramble around to the base of the West Ridge; some parties report one more short rappel from that notch to regain the south-face base. Total time from summit back to packs is roughly 2 hours in a typical trip report.

before.belay: Belay on knobby ground just left of the top of the chimney.
before.notes: Climb the left-side chimney between two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; move left atop the chimney onto knobby terrain to belay.
Sustained knobby face, slabs, and cracks up toward a gully/chimney system; route-finding is somewhat ambiguous through this stretch on the way to Snafflehound Ledge.
Traverse right across the obvious Snafflehound Ledge to a small tree, then a short steep step to the base of the crux pitch.
Route crux: a shallow left-facing dihedral forces you right until an overhang forces a step-across left into a flaring jam crack; eases above the bulge on face holds and chicken-heads.
Crack system/steep gully bypassing a chockstone on the left to the small notch east of the summit horn; watch for loose blocks in the gully.

Delicate friction traverse on a ramp finishing on a good jam crack to the summit; a harder 5.10a thin-hands splitter variant climbs straight out of the notch for parties wanting more technical finish.

before.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core to the chimney left of the two Vs
before.notes:
The Core Enchantments approach, shared with every other line on this face: Stuart Lake trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail to the Colchuck Lake Trail junction, across Mountaineer Creek and up to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, then the boulder field at the south end and Aasgard Pass — 2,000 ft in 1.25 miles of loose scree, hazardous under lingering snow into early July because of a creek and moat hidden beneath it.

From the pass, cross-country north past Tranquil and Isolation lakes toward Gnome Tarn and the base of the south face, roughly 7.5 to 8 miles and 4,600 ft one way.

If the standard trailhead or the pass is shut — wildfire closures have done this — the Snow Lakes trail reaches the same face by a longer and less direct line past Lake Viviane and a climbers' path onto the south side of the peak. One party clocked that version at about ten miles and 6,000 ft.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: loose scree, and a hidden creek and moat under snow into early July
Avalanche on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country travel for the final approach
Six rappels down the north face on ageing natural anchors — carry extra tat
A possible extra rappel from the West Ridge notch to regain the south-face base
Snafflehounds at the base will eat gear left unattended
before.baseFinding:
Look for two large Vs and start in the chimney to their left. That is the whole identification, it is published in exactly those terms, and the accompanying note is that you cannot miss it. Two prominent V-shaped features on the south face; the route's first pitch takes the chimney immediately left of them.

Confirm with the first pitch itself: from the chimney you move left and climb up on knobs to a belay, at about 5.7. Knobs after a leftward move out of a chimney is the signature. If you are pulling straight up out of the chimney with no traverse, look again.

Position relative to its neighbour, which is the check that catches the common error: this route is to the climber's right of the classic south-face line. So if you are at the middle of the base of the face, you are one route too far left. Walk right until the two Vs are on your right-hand side and you are at a chimney.

And a distance check on the route as a whole: seven pitches, about 650 ft, running 5.5 to 5.9, with a long chimney-gully crossing to a big ledge partway up and a forced rightward dihedral as the crux. A four- or five-pitch route ending on the West Ridge is one of the shorter lines on the left flank, not this.

In cloud, when you cannot see the Vs from a distance, walk the foot of the face and count chimneys rather than guessing: the Vs are large features and they are visible from close under them even when the summit is not.

before: The route follows a ledge system extending from the center of the south face rightward into a series of chimneys and wide cracks. Lower pitches (roughly pitches 2-4) involve scrambling and chimney climbing from 5.6-5.7 up to 5.8+ on somewhat loose rock. The crux, pitch 5, is a pleasant finger-and-hands crack with good protection, finishing with a fist jam through a small overhang. Some parties continue up the final West Face 5.6 slab pitch to reach the true summit rather than stopping at the top of pitch 6.

before.name: SR-20 Hairpin / Pond Pullout (east of Washington Pass)
before.note: Same pullout used for the Kangaroo Temple/West Route approach on the outside of the SR-20 hairpin; no permit required.
before.directions: Park in the pullout at the hairpin turn on SR-20, a short distance east of Washington Pass at around 5,100 feet — the same roadside pullout used for the nearby West Route approach on Kangaroo Temple. No permit is required to park or climb from here.

before.name: Early Winters Creek (West Face turnoff)
before.note: The West Face line crosses the creek near here; for the south face, stay on the climbers' trail on the west side of the creek and keep heading up-valley.
before.directions: From the pullout, walk south into the trees to pick up the cairned climbers' trail and follow it along the west side of Early Winters Creek for about half a mile, to where the West Face line crosses the creek at the edge of the talus field. For this route, do not cross here.

before.name: Big Kangaroo Summit
before.note: Final 20-ft exposed, unprotected slab move tops out at the small summit bolt shared with the Southwest Rib/West Route.
before.directions: Stay on the climbers' trail on the west side of the creek and keep heading up-valley through talus and boulder fields to the head of the basin. Turn left (east) and climb broad scree to the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon, aiming for the col midway between them rather than the steeper notch nearer Half Moon, and cross into the basin under Big Kangaroo's south wall. Start up the obvious central ramp and climb six pitches of ramps, chimneys and cracks, 5.4 to 5.9+. From the last belay scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches, finishing with the exposed, essentially unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old 1/4-inch bolt.

before: Do not plan to rappel the Beckey-Tate line itself — while it's technically possible with two ropes (roughly five or six rappels off slings and trees), the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, making rope-stuck and rockfall risk high; most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead, from the top of the route scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which stands a few hundred feet higher. To tag it, drop about 150 ft of scree on the far side, cross north into the West Route gully and climb its short pitches to the unprotected 5.6 summit slab (protected by a single old bolt), which is downclimbed or top-roped; then descend the shared gully: two slung-block anchors get you down with one or two single-rope rappels (a 60m rope is sufficient either way) through the steep/loose upper gully, after which it's a scree-and-snow walk/glissade down the gully back to the approach basin, across Early Winters Creek, and out the climbers' trail to the Hairpin Turn. Expect the full descent to take a couple of hours; keep helmets on throughout given the loose rock in the gully.

before.name: The Hairpin turnout, staying west of the creek longer than the West Face line, then over the Half Moon col into the south basin
before.notes:
From the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20, follow the cairned climbers' trail south along the west side of Early Winters Creek toward Kangaroo Temple and Wallaby Peak, but stay on the trail, on the right or west side of the creek, longer than the west face line does. Do not cross the creek where that route splits off.

Continue up-valley as the trail fades into open talus and boulder fields, then work toward the head of the basin. Roughly 2 miles and 2,440 ft one-way to the base, with 2.5-5 hours a reasonable estimate given the route-finding through boulder fields. Noticeably longer and more sustained than the standard West Face gully route.
hazards: Talus hopping and route-finding through boulder fields for 2 miles
A lot of large loose rock on the route, making rappelling it inadvisable
An exposed unprotected 5.6 slab move past a single old bolt if tagging the true summit
A steep, loose upper gully on the shared descent
Snow lingering in the approach basin and the gullies near the top of the route in early season
before.baseFinding:
Cut left, east, toward the low point on the ridge between Big Kangaroo and Half Moon. That col drops and traverses you into the south-facing basin directly below Big Kangaroo's south wall.

Arrival at the route itself is visual and unambiguous when you can see the wall: the Beckey-Tate's obvious central ramp-and-ledge system splits the face. A single ramp system running up the middle of a south wall, splitting it, is the line.

So the order of finds is: stay west of the creek, reach the head of the basin, cut east to the Half Moon col, drop into the south basin, then look for the ramp splitting the middle of the wall.

The negative test against the west face, which is the commonest error from this car: the west face route crosses Early Winters Creek after only half a mile, at the edge of the talus field, and takes a broad shallow west-facing gully with a chockstone in it. If you crossed the creek early and are looking at a chockstone, you are on the west side of the mountain.

And against the other south-face lines, which share this basin: Kearney-Thomas crosses the creek and ascends the prominent gully system taking the left fork at the high Y-junction. Going down under starts at the Beckey-Tate base and then traverses right across overlaps to its own start ledge. Skinny Start is about 30 metres right of the Kearney-Thomas start. So on this wall: the central ramp is Beckey-Tate, and everything else is measured from either it or Kearney-Thomas.

Descent is not down this route, and the reason matters: rappelling the Beckey-Tate is technically possible with two ropes, roughly five to six rappels off slings and trees, but the route wanders and holds a lot of large loose rock, so rope-stuck and rockfall risk is high and most parties explicitly avoid it. Instead scramble about 20 ft up and left to the notch between the south face and the true summit, which is a few hundred feet higher, and descend the gully from there.

before: Beyond Redlining climbs the West Face of Vega North Tower (Eros Tower) in 11 sustained pitches (1,200 ft, Grade IV 5.10+; 8 of 11 pitches are 5.10 or harder), topping out on the same summit as Mile High Club. Established by Rad Roberts and Kurt Hicks in July 2020, it is a full grade harder, longer, and more committing than Mile High Club — generally excellent rock, with one notably polished, more run-out pitch (P3) and a long 55m opening pitch.

Drive to the Sunrise Mine trailhead (Mountain Loop Highway, Forest Road 4065) and start up the Sunrise Mine Trail. Follow it about 2.5 miles, gaining to roughly 4,300 ft, to the last major switchback before the trail begins its final zigzag up toward Headlee Pass — this is the turnoff point, not the pass itself. Leave the maintained trail here and pick up a cairned traverse heading northeast across open talus toward Vega North Tower (also called Eros Tower). The line of cairns crosses two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees, passing just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees. This talus traverse is the shared approach for Mile High Club, Marvin's Ear, and Beyond Redlining, so cairns and a boot path are well established in season, but talus can be loose and slow going with a pack. A reliable fresh-water seep is at a red-rock outcrop in the Mile High gully, roughly at the base of the formation — worth topping off here since there's no water higher on the wall. Beyond Redlining's start is on the dark gray face directly above the two largest boulders at the base of the tower, just left of (west of) Mile High Club's start. Expect lingering steep snow against the base in early season, which can make the last stretch of the talus approach and the transition onto rock its own small crux.

before.notes: Climbs the dark gray face above the two largest boulders at the tower's base, with multiple cruxes leading to a roof breached on the right side.
Navigate a bulge, ascend a rib, and traverse a steep slab; watch for loose rock in the approach gully below.
A more serious pitch than the grade suggests: polished rock, sparse bolts, and few positive holds on a left-trending ramp.
Low-angle terrain traversing above a large ledge to the belay.

before.belay: On the large ledge system at the top of the featured vertical face.
before.notes: Three fun cruxes lead to a featured, vertical finish on a large ledge system.
A steep face with a tricky bulge at an orange band; extend draws to manage rope drag. An unfinished, harder direct variant exists here but is not recommended as bolted.
A fun slab with easy runout, then steep athletic moves and a punchy crux at a bulge.

before.belay: Just above the large roof, at the first anchor you reach.
before.notes: A looming, very airy headwall with a wild corner past a couple of roofs.
Steeper than it looks: steep jugs, side-pulls, and jams on an overhanging face.
A golden, featured slab with a crux bulge, then an arête past a curious 'Mouth' feature.
A tricky boulder problem at the top of the pillar — the route's final and hardest crux — just below the summit shared with Mile High Club.

before: Mountain Project route page confirms: '60 meter rope,' '17 quickdraws,' and '3-6 alpine draws to reduce rope drag'; a 70m rope is a helpful-but-not-mandatory retreat option.

before.pull: A rope end has jammed in a crack on the right side of this rappel, forcing the party to climb back up the other strand to free it - and the ground you would climb to reach it is loose. Watch where the ends land and pull away from the crack.
before.notes: First rappel off the shared summit down to the P7 anchor on Mile High Club's line; single 60m rope reaches comfortably.
before.anchor: summit rap rings, station ~8ft south of summit bolts and ~4ft off the ground
hazards: The edge below this station has cut a rope badly enough that the party had to chop it in half and retire it. The route page says the edge has since been ground down; the Beyond Redlining page still tells you exactly where to lay the rope, so treat it as live

A hard pendulum. The first-ascent advice is to lower to the large flake and walk left to the belay rather than rappelling free; a 2025 party swung hard right into a separate rock face on this rappel, on both of their visits
The nuts on these rap rings have been found loose - check them before you weight the station

Rappelling Beyond Redlining's own line is what this station exists to avoid: its first pitch is over 50 m, several pitches angle substantially left or right, and it needs angling rappels off single bolts, many of which only reach the next anchor on rope stretch
before.station: Not on Beyond Redlining. From the shared summit, walk about 50 ft over to Mile High Club's top station: the rap rings are set back from the top of the route, and the place to lay the rope is the least sharp part of the edge roughly 8 ft south of the bolts and about 4 ft off the ground. Toss just left of the crest, then angle down to the lower anchor at the base of pitch 7. From here the whole descent stays about 10-15 ft skier's left of the bolt line, and for most pitches you can see the climbing anchors from the rap anchors.

before.notes: A face-descent rappel down to the P6 anchor.
hazards: Dropping to the dihedral-top anchor instead is a specific, named mistake - the station you want is above and left of it
The published reason for tossing left is that parties climb directly below: keep the rope and anything you knock loose off them
before.station: Toss the rope slightly left of the bolt line rather than straight down. Rappel the pitch-6 face, then move to a rap anchor about 10 ft skier's left and 10 ft above the anchor at the top of the dihedral pitch. Do not continue to the top of the dihedral pitch.

before.notes: A short rappel down to a ledge at P5; source explicitly flags this one as short.
hazards: Free-hanging above a ledge, so you arrive spinning onto a stance rather than sliding onto it
before.station: A short rappel from the pitch-5 station to an anchor on a ledge off to the side of the dihedral pitch. It is free-hanging above the ledge.

before.notes: Drops to P4, where one of two available anchor options is used.
hazards: Most stations on this route have two anchors a few feet apart so ascending and descending parties do not share one - taking the wrong one puts you on top of climbers
Rope thrown from here lands on anyone on pitch 4 below
before.station: Two anchors are available here; take the skier's-left one where you can, which keeps you off the climbing line.

before.pull: A rope has been stuck in a crack pulling from the pitch-3 rap anchors; pull away from the crack. Feed the rope through the cedar bushes rather than throwing it.
before.notes: The most commonly botched rappel on the descent — aim for a 10-ft-tall tree roughly 15 ft skier's-left of the climbing line; a hidden intermediate anchor is tucked in cedar bushes just below the visible upper-P3 station.
hazards: The route page states it outright: do not rappel down the vertical face on a single rope, because you will not reach the next anchors. Parties who miss it end up either doing two double-rope rappels from the top of pitch 3 or, on an 80 m, nearly reaching the pitch-2 anchors and then having to scramble across exposed ground
One party that missed it could not retrieve their rope at all - the pull angle around the intervening features made it stick and recovering it was judged unsafe
The tree the beta says will be flagged has never been flagged; years later the beta still only promises that it will be flagged soon
before.station: The confusing one, and by a wide margin the most-reported problem on this descent. From the pitch-4 anchor, pass through cedar bushes directly below the station and rappel the low-angle upper part of pitch 3 - it is mostly walking. Aim for a tree about 10 ft tall standing roughly 15 ft skier's left of the climbing line; the intermediate anchor is tucked into a nook just below that tree. Look for it right where the ground turns from slabby to vertical. You cannot see this anchor on the way up, so it cannot be scouted on the climb; parties have found chalk arrows pointing at it.

before.notes: Continues down to a lower-P3 anchor, landing on a large ledge.
hazards: This is the vertical face the station above exists to get you onto safely; it is the ground you would be stranded above having missed the nook
before.station: From the nook anchor, rappel the vertical section at the start of pitch 3 down to a large ledge, and set up at either of the anchors at the top of pitch 2 - the skier's-left one if it is free.

before.notes: Drops to the P2 anchor.
hazards: Parties consistently record being surprised that the last anchor before the ground is a separate one, offset from the climbing anchor
before.station: The station is NOT the pitch-1 climbing anchor, which is what people expect and head for. The rap anchor is about 10 ft down and 10-15 ft skier's left of the pitch-1 belay anchor.

before.pull: Consider staying on rappel and walking back to the belay bolt at the start of the route, then pulling the rope from there.
before.notes: Final rappel(s) via the P2 and P1 anchors bring you to the base of the route.
hazards: Do not treat the base of the route as the ground - the ledge you land on is exposed and hundreds of feet up
The gully to climber's right throws natural rockfall onto the start of the scramble; keep helmets on until you are clear of it, especially with parties above
before.station: Final rappel to the base of the route. The starting ledge is several hundred feet above the ground and quite exposed.

before.name: Sunrise Mine Trail to the cairned talus traverse
before.notes: Sunrise Mine trailhead, then the trail for about two and a half miles through the two unbridged creek crossings and up through forest to the last major switchback before the final zigzags toward the pass — leave the trail there, not at the pass. A cairned traverse then runs northeast across talus toward the tower, crossing two separate talus fields separated by strips of subalpine trees and passing just above a large flat-topped boulder near the first stand of trees. The boot path is well established in season because three routes share it. Top up water at the seep by the red-rock outcrop in the gully; there is none higher.
before.season: June to September. This face is west-facing and stays shaded and cold until roughly midday; significant snow can lie at the base from December through May.
hazards: Two unbridged creek crossings in the first mile
Loose talus on the traverse and party-inflicted rockfall across several pitches
West-facing and shaded until around midday, so cold starts are the norm
Steep snow against the base into early summer, which makes the last stretch of talus and the step onto rock its own small crux
The fifty-five-metre opening pitch commits you before any real bail option
before.baseFinding: Stay on the talus at the foot of the tower's west face — do not go up into the red gully on the right. Find the two largest boulders at the base of the tower and look straight up: the start is on the dark grey face directly above them. The confirmation is the bolt count — the first pitch is a single fifty-five-metre rope length with sixteen bolts in it, so if what you are under is short, or has only a handful of bolts, it is not this. Negative markers: if you have scrambled up and left on loose ledges past a lone fir to a single bolt on a narrow ledge, you are on the arete route one line to your right, which shares this tower's summit but not its face; if you left the traverse into a gully on the right-hand side of the tower and gained a notch on the skyline ridge through cedar and heather, you are on the next tower along.

before: Leave the Wildhorse Creek Trail at about 5,400 ft, directly west of the summit. Climb east through meadows, going around the rock bands rather than through them, to gain the west ridge. Follow the ridge east toward the main summit ridge. Short of the summit headwall, turn north and traverse below it, then scramble up blocky Class 2-3 ledges to the summit pinnacle. The last moves are exposed; pick the easiest line and test holds, as the rock is broken and loose in places.

before.trailheadDirection: From Highway 20 in Winthrop, turn north on West Chewuch Road, go straight at the junction with East Chewuch Road after about 7 miles, continue about 2.5 miles as the road becomes Forest Road 51, then turn left onto Forest Road 5130 (Eightmile Road) and follow it about 12 miles to the trailhead pullout on the right.

before.name: South Fork log crossing to Dry Creek basin
before.notes:
Two starts reach the same ground: the Big Four Picnic Area / Ice Caves trailhead at about 1,640 ft, or the Mount Dickerman trailhead across the highway, which lands you nearer the drainage. Either way, walk to the South Fork Stillaguamish and hunt up and down the bank for a large sound log — there is no bridge, but several substantial logs are usually available.

On the south bank travel southeasterly through open forest, roughly a mile, with heavy log debris and tall vegetation obstructing the line. A dense band of slide alder guards the forest edge before the creek; turning west generally avoids most of it.

Follow the broad, smoother bed of Dry Creek upward. Water surfaces around 2,200 ft. The headwall ahead carries a visible waterfall. Above the headwall, the upper basin opens onto talus.
before.season: Late spring to summer — after the couloir snow consolidates, before it melts to bare loose rock
hazards: Unbridged log crossing of the South Fork Stillaguamish
Dense slide alder at the forest edge below Dry Creek
Steep, icy, committing main couloir with no escape once started
Exposed class 4 on the red slabs
Heavy blowdown and pathless forest travel — no trail of any kind
before.baseFinding:
There is more than one gully in the headwall and the choice matters. The northernmost gully is the winter line. In dry conditions take the one trending west toward the upper basin, gained by a series of class 3-4 ledges and ramps rather than by a snow chute; in snow conditions the hidden chute goes instead.

From the upper basin, walk south across several gullies before you commit. The correct main couloir is the one that is noticeably narrower than the ones you crossed to get there, and it is the point where crampons go on. A gully you can stroll into without committing is not it — the right one is steep and offers no reprieve from the first steps. Higher, a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave, from where a rightward class 4 traverse on red slabby rock gains the South Ridge of the Main Peak; red rock underfoot on that traverse is the confirmation.

before.label: Main couloir
before.notes: From the upper basin, walk south across several gullies to the narrower main couloir and climb it to its head.

before.label: Red slabs to the summit ridge
before.notes: Above the couloir, a steep gully or snowfinger leads to a small cave; an exposed class 4 traverse right on red slabs gains the summit ridge.

before: Big Four Mountain's first ascent was made July 19, 1931 by Forest Farr and Art Winder via the northwest ridge -- the original route to the summit. As with the mountain's other lines, this route begins from the Big Four viewpoint/ice caves trail approach on the Mountain Loop Highway.

First climbed March 2, 1996 by Bart Paull and Doug Littauer in a fast, ultralight, ~9-hour push with no bivy gear. The route starts up an 'ice ribbon' on the initial slabs (thin ice at roughly 65 degrees with a short 85-degree step), continues through the main couloir's three steps of mostly moderate terrain, and hits its crux about three-quarters height: a 100-foot pitch of near-vertical ice leading to steep, often runnelled snow. The upper section mixes rotten ice, shale, and drytooling moves up to roughly 95-degree angles before summit cornices, which may require tunneling through.

The route tops out on the summit ridge well west of the true summit. Descent goes northwest, via rappels and steep downclimbing, to the col between Big Four and Hall Peak; from there, multiple tree-anchored rappels lead back down through the North Face bowl to the base of the face. Careful navigation is essential -- parties have mistakenly descended south instead of northwest in poor visibility.

before.notes: Climb a ribbon of ice on the initial slabs, reached through a break in the lower cliffs right of the steepest part of the headwall. On the first ascent it was about 65°, half an inch to an inch thick and too thin for protection or belays. It thinned to 5.8 mixed moves on edges, then a short near-vertical step on a thicker tongue, then more thin 65° ice to the bowl.

Low-angle snow crosses the bowl toward the couloir, which cuts through shale bands several gullies right of the north rib. The bowl steepens to about 35° on the avalanche fan below the couloir. Snow ranges from névé to wind crust over powder, and rockfall and slides come down this fan, so do not linger.

The first of three steeper steps in the couloir: about two pitches of névé and water ice at roughly 75°, narrowing in one place to a slot about three feet wide with fat ice at the back. Protection is available here. About 300 ft of steeper ground in all brings you to the top of the step.

Rotten shale, snow mushrooms and thin, strange ice. It starts on good 75° ice, then the ice gives out to powder over shale and the picks have to be dragged through snow until they catch. Protection and belay options are very poor, and the angle drops to about 60° on thicker ice at the top.

At about three-quarters height, the third and steepest step. In good conditions it is a near-vertical ice pitch leading to steep, often runnelled snow. In lean conditions it has gone as rotten ice over shale at 80–95°, with drytooling and a knifeblade in a shale seam as the main protection. The belay at its base is poor.

About 1,000 ft of mostly névé and ice remains above the third step and can be simul-climbed with occasional screws. In the last few hundred feet the snow can turn unconsolidated and give no protection, which makes this exposed upper slope one of the most serious parts of the route. A short mixed section sits just below the cornices.

Summit cornices can overhang the face by about six feet. The first ascent cut a tunnel through them with an adze to reach the ridge. The route tops out on the summit ridge well west of the true summit, where a boulder offers a solid cam anchor for bringing up the second.

before: First climbed July 25, 1972 by Ben Guydelkon and Ron Miller as a new line on Big Four's north side. From the end of the ice-caves trail, the party traversed to the northeast side of the first tower to a prominent gully; climbing this gully let them work west onto and up the first tower. They rappelled into a notch, climbed two more towers, then finished with rock scrambling leading to a long, steep, exposed snowfield to the summit.

before.notes: Ascend the prominent gully on the NE side to the first tower
Work west onto and up the first tower
Rappel into the notch between towers
Continue climbing the remaining two towers
Long, steep, exposed snowfield leads to the summit
